content: There is concern regarding the risk of pregnancy when an intrauterine device (IUD) is removed during a menstrual cycle in which sexual intercourse has already occurred. To mitigate this risk, it is recommended to leave the IUD in place until the next menstrual period. Progestogen-only pills (POPs) require approximately 48 hours of use to achieve contraceptive effects on cervical mucus. However, the time required for progestogen-only injectables (POIs) to exert a similar effect remains uncertain. The Guideline Development Group (GDG) noted that the efficacy of subcutaneous depot medroxyprogesterone acetate (DMPA-SC) is maintained when administered in the upper arm, which may be preferable for some women compared to injections in the abdomen or thigh. For healthy women, no mandatory examinations or tests are required before initiating POIs. However, blood pressure screening is desirable prior to initiation. In settings where blood pressure measurements are unavailable, women should not be denied access to POIs solely due to the inability to measure blood pressure. Breast examinations, pelvic/genital examinations, cervical cancer screening, routine laboratory tests, hemoglobin tests, and STI/HIV screenings are not essential for the safe and effective use of DMPA-SC. These tests may be appropriate for preventive health care or diagnosing suspected medical conditions but are not mandatory for contraceptive initiation. DMPA injections should be administered every three months, while norethisterone enanthate (NET-EN) injections should be given every two months. Early injections can be administered up to two weeks before the scheduled date, and late injections can be given up to four weeks after the scheduled date for DMPA and two weeks for NET-EN without requiring additional contraceptive protection. If the delay exceeds these timeframes, the injection can still be given if it is reasonably certain the woman is not pregnant. In such cases, the woman should abstain from sexual activity or use additional contraceptive protection for the next seven days and may consider emergency contraception if appropriate. Switching between DMPA and NET-EN is not recommended but can be done at the time of the next scheduled injection if necessary. If the type or timing of the previous injectable contraceptive is unknown, the injection can be given if pregnancy is reasonably excluded, with the same precautions regarding abstinence or additional protection for seven days. Menstrual abnormalities, such as amenorrhea, spotting, or heavy bleeding, are common with POI use. Amenorrhea does not require medical treatment, and counseling is usually sufficient. Persistent spotting or bleeding should prompt an evaluation for gynecologic problems, and if identified, appropriate treatment or referral should be provided. If no underlying issues are found and the bleeding is unacceptable, short-term treatment with NSAIDs or hormonal drugs like ethinyl estradiol may be helpful. For heavy or prolonged bleeding, iron supplementation and dietary advice may be necessary to prevent anemia. Progestogen-only pills (POPs) can be initiated at any time if it is reasonably certain the woman is not pregnant. If started within five days of menstrual bleeding, no additional contraceptive protection is needed. If started later, abstinence or additional protection is required for two days. POPs can also be initiated immediately postpartum, post-abortion, or when switching from another hormonal method, provided the previous method was used consistently and correctly. When switching from a non-hormonal method, POPs can be started within five days of menstrual bleeding without additional protection. If started later, the same precautions regarding abstinence or additional protection for two days apply. For women switching from an IUD, the IUD can be removed if POPs are initiated within five days of menstrual bleeding. If initiated later, the IUD should remain in place until the next menstrual period if sexual activity has occurred during the cycle. The GDG emphasized the importance of counseling women about potential menstrual abnormalities before initiating POI use to alleviate concerns and encourage method continuation.
